system_message:
You are generating a synthetic but clinically grounded
conversation for exactly one hospital admission.

Rules:
1. Use only facts supported by the provided admission context.
2. The discharge notes are the backbone of the hospital-course
   narrative. Use them first.
3. The ordered problem list should shape the main clinical focus.
4. Radiology, procedures, microbiology, and the previous-admission
   summary are supporting context, not a checklist.
5. Not every packet item needs to appear in the conversation.
6. Speakers must be exactly: Doctor and Patient.
7. Every conversation line must contain:
   - turn number
   - exact timestamp
   - speaker
   - text
8. Timestamps must be monotonically increasing and stay within the
   admission start and admission end times.
9. Keep the conversation medically plausible and understandable to
   a patient.
10. Use short natural exchanges, patient questions, clarifications,
    explanations, reassurance, and follow-up discussion.
11. Do not invent unsupported diagnoses, procedures, test findings,
    or outcomes.
12. Do not mention the dataset, packet, note types, or that the
    conversation is synthetic.
13. Generate the conversation first, then write the summary strictly from the generated conversation_lines.
14. Every claim in summary.summary_paragraph and every item in summary.problems must be explicitly supported by the conversation_lines.
15. Return output that exactly matches the required JSON schema.
task_message:
Generate one rich patient-doctor conversation for this admission and one admission summary.

Generation guidance:
- Approximate stay length: 2 day(s).
- Recommended turn range: 40-60 turns.
- Exact admission window: 2170-09-28 23:55:00 to 2170-09-30 19:54:00.
- Focus first on the discharge-note storyline and the core admission problems.
- Use radiology, procedures, and microbiology only as supporting detail when they help the story.
- Do not try to mention every packet item.
- Let the conversation unfold across admission, mid-course updates, and discharge planning.
- Prefer many short natural exchanges over a few long summary turns.
- The patient should ask questions, express concerns, seek clarification, and respond to updates throughout the stay.
- The doctor should explain results, treatment changes, progress, and follow-up in multiple conversational beats over time.
- You may paraphrase and add natural conversational glue, but do not invent unsupported diagnoses, procedures, findings, or outcomes.
- Generate the conversation first, then derive the final summary only from the conversation_lines you wrote.
- The final summary must contain admission start time, admission end time, one paragraph summary, and a list of problems.
- Final self-check before returning JSON: turn_number contiguous from 1; conversation_lines.time nondecreasing and inside the exact admission window; summary.admission_start and summary.admission_end copied exactly from the packet; no conversation line has empty text.

previous_admission_summary_used.summary_paragraph: A female patient with a history of endometriosis was admitted for acute-on-chronic pelvic pain characterized by sharp, intermittent left lower quadrant pain radiating to the rectum and left leg. Initial vitals showed tachycardia due to pain, which resolved with treatment. Physical exam revealed mild left lower quadrant tenderness without peritoneal signs. A pelvic ultrasound showed a normal uterus and ovaries with no evidence of torsion or free fluid. Laboratory results, including WBC and lactate, were within acceptable limits, ruling out infection or ischemia. Pain was managed with intravenous and oral medications, including Dilaudid, gabapentin, ibuprofen, tramadol, and acetaminophen. The patient improved significantly, tolerated oral medications, and was discharged home on hospital day one with a stable condition. Follow-up was arranged with her gynecologist, and she was advised to monitor for warning signs including fever, severe pain, or abnormal bleeding.
problems: Migraine, unspecified, without mention of intractable migraine without mention of status migrainosus

radiology_notes.text:
INDICATION:  History of endometriosis, abdominal pain, now with elevated
lactate and worsening pain.  Assess for intra-abdominal infection.

COMPARISON:  Comparison is made to CT abdomen and pelvis performed ___.

TECHNIQUE:  Contrast-enhanced axial images were obtained from the lung bases
to pelvic outlet.  Coronal and sagittal reformations are provided.

FINDINGS:  Limited assessment of the lung bases demonstrate no opacifications
or pleural effusions.

The liver is homogeneous in attenuation without discrete masses or lesions. 
There is no intra- or extra-hepatic biliary ductal dilatation.  The
gallbladder, pancreas, spleen, bilateral adrenal glands, kidneys, ureter and
bladder are unremarkable.

The stomach is otherwise unremarkable.  The small bowel contains multiple
non-distended fluid-filled loops of bowel without associated bowel wall
thickening or abnormal enhancement. In addition, there is slight prominence of
the mesenteric vessels which may relate to the same process.  Findings may be
due to diarrhea in the setting of nonspecific enterovirus.  The large bowel is
overall collapsed and thus poorly assessed though there is no definite
evidence of colitis.

The uterus and adnexa are grossly unremarkable.  A 12mm left ovarian cyst is
slighlty hyperdense possibly due to hemorrhagic content.

The portal venous system as well as the celiac and superior mesenteric
arteries are widely patent.  There is no free air or fluid within the abdomen.
Scattered mesenteric lymph nodes do not meet CT criteria for pathologic
enlargement.  
No suspicious lytic or blastic lesions present.

IMPRESSION:  
1. Multiple fluid-filled loops of non-distended small bowel without bowel wall
thickening or abnormal enhancement.  Slight hypervascularity of the mesentery.
Findings are nonspecific but may relate to diarrhea in the setting of
enterovirus.  Please correlate clinically.  The colon is collapsed and thus
not well evaluated, though there are no findings to suggest colitis, ischemia
or otherwise.

2. Uterus and adnexa are normal. 12mm left ovarian cyst is slightly hyperdense
likely representing hemorrhagic content. 

Findings including potential hemorrhagic ovarian cyst were discussed with Dr.
___ at 4:00 AM on ___ via telephone ___ minutes after interpretation.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Hi, I'm Dr. Lee, one of the gynecology doctors. You're here because of severe left lower abdominal pain. Can you tell me more about it?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes, it started yesterday at noon. It’s sharp and constant, and it radiates down to my left leg and into my rectum. I’ve been having endometriosis pain for years, but this feels worse.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I see. You mentioned you tried gabapentin and tramadol, but no relief?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Right. I took my usual doses, but nothing helped. I was shaking and couldn’t sit still. That’s why I came in.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your heart rate was very high when you arrived—158. That’s likely from the pain. We’ve given you dilaudid, morphine, and other meds in the ER to help.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: It’s better now, but still aching. Is this another flare-up of my endometriosis?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s what it looks like. But because your lactate was elevated, we wanted to rule out something serious like an infection or bowel issue, so we did a CT scan.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Lactate? I’ve heard that before. Does that mean my body was under stress?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Exactly. Elevated lactate can mean your tissues aren’t getting enough oxygen, often from severe pain or infection. But your CT came back mostly normal.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Mostly? What wasn’t normal?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: There’s a small 12mm cyst on your left ovary that looks like it might have a little blood in it—what we call a hemorrhagic cyst. But your uterus and other organs look fine.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Could that be causing the pain?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Possibly, but it’s small. More likely, this is a flare of your endometriosis. The CT didn’t show infection, blockage, or anything else dangerous.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay, that makes sense. What’s next?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll keep managing your pain with IV medications for now. Once you can tolerate pills, we’ll switch you to oral meds.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. How’s the pain today?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Better. Still there, but I can lie still now. Did the labs show anything?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your potassium was a bit low at 3.0, so we’re watching that. Glucose was high at 197, but that can happen with stress. No signs of infection in your blood or urine.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’m on lithium—could that affect my labs?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It can, but your levels weren’t checked this admission. We’ll make sure your psychiatrist keeps an eye on it.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thanks. I’ve been on it for my bipolar disorder and it helps.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good. We’re adjusting your pain meds too. Your gabapentin dose is being increased to 400mg four times a day.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s higher than before. Will it make me sleepy?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It might at first, but we’re doing it gradually. We’re also adding tizanidine, a muscle relaxant, three times a day.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay. And tramadol for breakthrough pain?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, tramadol as needed every six hours. But don’t take more than four in 24 hours, and no alcohol with it.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re doing well. We’re going to start you on norethindrone acetate, a progesterone, to help prevent future endometriosis flares.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Is that like birth control?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It’s similar. It won’t prevent pregnancy completely, but it helps suppress endometriosis activity.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’m not trying to get pregnant, so that’s fine. What about the Lupron I heard about?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’ll get a Lupron injection before you go home. It helps reduce endometriosis symptoms long-term by lowering estrogen.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ve had that before. It helped, but I had hot flashes.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll monitor that. It’s usually worth it for the pain relief. You’re also staying on omeprazole for your reflux and your asthma inhalers.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’ve been stable all day, and your pain is much better. We think you’re ready to go home tomorrow.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s great. What should I watch for at home?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Call if you have a fever over 100.4, severe pain, heavy vaginal bleeding—more than one pad per hour—or trouble urinating.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And constipation? The narcotics usually cause that.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Exactly. Take a stool softener like Colace daily. And don’t drive on narcotics. Also, no alcohol or sedatives with them.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re cleared to go home. You got the Lupron shot this morning, and all your meds are ready.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thank you. I feel so much better. I’ll follow up with my gynecologist?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, they’ll get your records. Keep taking everything as prescribed and call if anything worsens.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I will. I’m glad this wasn’t something more serious.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re glad too. Take care, and rest well at home.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I will. Thanks again, Dr. Lee.

summary.summary_paragraph: A female patient with a history of endometriosis was admitted for severe left lower quadrant pain radiating to the rectum and left leg, consistent with an acute exacerbation of chronic endometriosis pain. Initial presentation included tachycardia with a heart rate of 158, attributed to pain. A CT scan was performed due to elevated lactate, revealing a small hemorrhagic ovarian cyst but no evidence of infection, ischemia, or other acute intra-abdominal pathology. Pain was managed with intravenous dilaudid, morphine, and toradol, followed by transition to oral medications. The gabapentin dose was increased, tizanidine was added, and the patient received a Lupron injection prior to discharge. She improved significantly, remained stable, and was discharged home with follow-up instructions and new prescriptions. No procedures were performed during the admission.
problems: Migraine, unspecified, without mention of intractable migraine without mention of status migrainosus
